title: Celery Soup
source_title: The Three Rivers Cook Book (reprint, with supplement), King's Daughters Society
text: Cut a bunch of celery and boil it thoroughly one hour. Add one quart of chicken broth, one cup sweet cream, pepper and salt.
modern: Chop one head of celery and simmer it in a little salted water about an hour, until very soft (blend it smooth if you like). Add 4 cups chicken broth and 1 cup heavy or light cream, heat through without boiling, and season with salt and pepper.
note: Read on the page scan (printed page 2). Digitized by Michigan State University Libraries; PDF of whole book: https://archive.lib.msu.edu/DMC/Michigan%20Cookbook%20Storage/PDFs/ja11a006.pdf . The year 1896 comes from MSU's folder name; no date was seen on the pages read. Advertisers on the page footers are Three Rivers businesses.

title: Blue Grass Corn Pudding
source_title: New Crumbs of Comfort: A Cook Book, compiled by the Ladies of St. Luke's Church
text: For quart pan size: 12 ears corn; split corn down the grain (do not cut grains off cobb), then scrape; mix well with corn; 3 eggs well beaten, 1 lump butter, size egg, ½ teaspoonful of salt, just a little sugar, pepper to taste. 1 pint sweet milk. In medium hot oven, cook 25 minutes (till top of pudding is well brown). Serve as vegetable.
modern: Score down each row of kernels on 12 ears of fresh sweet corn and scrape the pulp and milk into a bowl (about 4 cups). Stir in 3 beaten eggs, 4 tablespoons melted butter ('size of an egg' is about 1/4 cup), 1/2 teaspoon salt, a pinch of sugar, pepper and 2 cups whole milk. Bake in a buttered 1 1/2- to 2-quart dish at 375°F for 25 to 35 minutes, until set and well browned on top.
note: Checked against the page scan (p. 45). Contributor was the rector of St. Luke's (named on the book's opening page). Third edition, Kalamazoo Publishing Co., Printers, 1906; Library of Congress copy.

title: Planked White Fish
source_title: New Crumbs of Comfort: A Cook Book, compiled by the Ladies of St. Luke's Church
text: Take a hardwood plank of well seasoned maple or oak about 1 1-2 feet long, 10 or 12 inches wide and 2 inches thick. Pour boiling water over it before using, until heated through. Split the fish open, bone, season well, lay upon the plank and bake. If the fish seems too dry, slices of salt pork may be placed upon the fish while baking. The fish should be served on the plank which may be garnished with rock salt or sprigs of parsley. The plank gives a peculiar delicious flavor which distinguishes it from fish baked in the ordinary way. Before serving cover fish with maitre de hotel sauce.
modern: Soak an untreated oak, maple or cedar cooking plank, then heat it in a 400°F oven. Lay a boned, butterflied whitefish skin-side down on the hot plank, season, top with a few strips of bacon if you like, and bake at 400°F for 15 to 20 minutes, until it flakes. Serve on the plank with lemon-parsley butter (maître d'hôtel butter).
note: Read in the Internet Archive OCR text (p. 32); two OCR punctuation slips corrected (comma after 'long', 'dry'). The book adds a note that planks could be bought at the 'Fair' in Chicago from fifteen cents up.

title: Rabbit Fricassee
source_title: New Crumbs of Comfort: A Cook Book, compiled by the Ladies of St. Luke's Church
text: Joint 2 carefully dressed rabbits, and place in a large dish of cold water with a handful of salt. Soak for 2 hours. Remove and rinse with fresh water, cover the bottom of a kettle with strips of salt pork (about ¼ of a lb.). When it is fried brown, slice on it a large onion and toss till light brown. Now add the jointed rabbit and stir till all are seared over; then add 1 qt. of boiling water, 1 tsp. salt and a pinch of red pepper. Place on the back of the range and simmer gently for 2 hours, or until perfectly tender. ... This is an excellent and economical dish in early winter when rabbits are in good condition.
modern: Brine two cut-up rabbits in salted water for 2 hours, then rinse. Brown 1/4 lb diced salt pork or bacon in a Dutch oven, add a sliced onion until golden, then sear the rabbit. Add 4 cups boiling water, 1 teaspoon salt and a pinch of cayenne, cover and simmer on low heat 1 1/2 to 2 hours until tender; thicken the broth for gravy and serve with currant jelly.
note: Read in the Internet Archive OCR text (p. 44); faithful excerpt (the omitted lines say to thicken and strain the gravy, garnish with lemon and parsley, and serve with currant jelly). OCR fraction '¼' should be checked against the scan before printing.

title: Apple Fritters
source_title: The Three Rivers Cook Book (reprint, with supplement), King's Daughters Society
text: Two egg, well beaten, one-half teaspoon salt, one cup milk, two and one-half cups of flour, two tablespoons of sugar, two tablespoons baking powder, four apples thickly sliced; flavor with vanilla. Fry as you would fried cakes and serve hot with maple syrup or a lemon sauce.
modern: Whisk 2 eggs, 1 cup milk, 2 tablespoons sugar, 1/2 teaspoon salt and a little vanilla; stir in 2 1/2 cups flour and 1 tablespoon baking powder (the original's 2 tablespoons is a lot for modern double-acting powder). Fold in 4 sliced apples, drop by spoonfuls into oil heated to 350–365°F, and fry until golden, 3–4 minutes. Serve hot with real maple syrup.
note: Read on the page scans (printed pp. 63–64; continuation at ja11a006p066.jpg). 'Two egg' is as printed.

title: Marlborough Pie
source_title: The Three Rivers Cook Book (reprint, with supplement), King's Daughters Society
text: Pare tart, mellow apples, quarter and take out seeds, stew in a little water until soft enough to put through a sieve. To twelve tablespoons of apple put same of sugar, six spoons melted butter, one-half pint of milk, the juice and rind of one lemon, some nutmeg. Bake in one crust, use whipped cream if you like it.
modern: Cook tart apples into a smooth sauce; measure 3/4 cup and mix with 3/4 cup sugar, 6 tablespoons melted butter, 1 cup milk, the zest and juice of a lemon and a grating of nutmeg (most cooks today also add 2–3 beaten eggs so the custard sets). Pour into an unbaked 9-inch crust and bake at 425°F for 10 minutes, then 350°F for 35–45 minutes until set. Top with whipped cream.
note: Read on the page scan (printed p. 72). The printed recipe has no eggs; the egg suggestion is a modern note only.

title: Cream Peach Pie
source_title: The Three Rivers Cook Book (reprint, with supplement), King's Daughters Society
text: Line a pie tin with rich paste, peel, halve and seed peaches enough to fill the pan, mix two tablespoons of flour with one cup of sugar and sprinkle over the peaches, fill the pan with thick sweet cream and bake until done. Canned peaches may be used or apples cut in small pieces.
modern: Fit a 9-inch pie plate with pastry and fill it with peeled peach halves, cut side up. Mix 1 cup sugar with 2 tablespoons flour, sprinkle over the fruit, and pour in about 1 cup heavy cream. Bake at 425°F for 15 minutes, then 350°F for 30–40 minutes, until the cream is set and lightly browned; cool before slicing.
note: Read on the page scans (printed pp. 71–72; continuation at ja11a006p074.jpg).

title: Boiled Huckleberry Pudding
source_title: New Crumbs of Comfort: A Cook Book, compiled by the Ladies of St. Luke's Church
text: Measure ¾ pt. of sifted flour; add to it 1 teaspoon baking powder, ½ salt spoon of salt. Sift thoroughly together. Stir a well beaten egg into ½ pt. milk, and stir this gradually into flour, making a smooth batter. Then stir in 1½ cups of berries; turn into a buttered mould, and steam, in enough boiling water to partly cover the mould, for 1 hour. Serve with hard or liquid sauce.
modern: Sift 1 1/2 cups flour with 1 teaspoon baking powder and 1/8 teaspoon salt; beat 1 egg into 1 cup milk and stir in to make a smooth batter, then fold in 1 1/2 cups huckleberries or wild blueberries. Pour into a buttered 1 1/2-quart pudding mold or heatproof bowl, cover tightly with foil, and steam on a rack in a covered pot of simmering water (halfway up the mold) for 1 hour. Serve warm with hard sauce or a sweet sauce.
note: Checked against the page scan (p. 123). A 'salt spoon' is about 1/4 teaspoon.

title: Pickle Peaches
source_title: New Crumbs of Comfort: A Cook Book, compiled by the Ladies of St. Luke's Church
text: 5 lbs. of peaches, 3 lbs. granulated sugar, ½ pint vinegar, 1 oz. cassia buds. Stick cassia buds into peaches. Make a good syrup with sugar and vinegar. Put fruit into hot syrup, and cook until tender. Place peaches in jar and pour over them the hot syrup.
modern: Peel 5 lb small, firm peaches and stud each with a few cassia buds (or whole cloves, or add cinnamon sticks to the syrup). Boil 6 cups sugar with 1 cup vinegar to a syrup, simmer the peaches in it until just tender, pack into hot jars and cover with the boiling syrup. Store in the refrigerator, or follow current USDA home-canning guidance and process in a water bath.
note: Read in the Internet Archive OCR text (p. 148); OCR 'y2' read as ½. A second Pickle Peaches recipe follows it on the same page.

title: Grape Juice
source_title: New Crumbs of Comfort: A Cook Book, compiled by the Ladies of St. Luke's Church
text: 10 lbs. Concord grapes, 2 qts. water. Put on stove, and cook until grapes burst open, then put in cheese cloth bags; let drain, and squeeze a little. Add to juice 2 coffeecups of sugar, and let boil 5 minutes; or until sugar is all dissolved. Put up in Mason cans.
modern: Simmer 10 lb stemmed Concord grapes with 8 cups water until the skins burst, about 10 minutes, then strain through a cheesecloth-lined colander or jelly bag, pressing lightly. Stir in about 2 cups sugar, boil 5 minutes, and pour into clean jars; refrigerate, freeze, or water-bath can following current USDA guidance.
note: Read in the Internet Archive OCR text (p. 155). A 'coffeecup' was about 1 cup.

title: Maple Creams
source_title: New Crumbs of Comfort: A Cook Book, compiled by the Ladies of St. Luke's Church
text: Cook 2 cups of pure maple syrup until a soft ball may be formed when dropped into cold water. Then add ¾ cup of sweet cream, and cook again till a soft ball is formed. Pour on marble slab, and proceed as with the fondant. Instead of mixing with the hands, it is better to cut into squares. Nuts may be stirred in with the wooden spatula.
modern: Boil 2 cups pure maple syrup to the soft-ball stage (235–240°F), stir in 3/4 cup heavy cream, and boil again to 235–240°F. Pour onto a buttered marble slab or baking sheet, let cool slightly, then work it with a wooden spatula until creamy and thick; stir in chopped nuts and cut into squares.
note: Read in the Internet Archive OCR text (p. 172); OCR '%' read as ¾ and 'Xuts'/'GEXE' as 'Nuts'/'Gene' – confirm the fraction on the scan before printing.

title: Popcorn Candy
source_title: Dr. Miles' Candy Book (Dr. Miles Medical Co. advertising booklet)
text: Four quarts popped corn, one cup molasses; put the molasses in an iron kettle and let it boil till it candies, then put in a lump of butter the size of half an egg, stir in the corn till well mixed; pour out in a buttered dripping pan and flatten out; when cold enough cut in square cakes and wrap in paraffine paper.
modern: Boil 1 cup molasses in a heavy pot to the hard-ball/soft-crack stage (about 260–270°F), stir in 2 tablespoons butter, then quickly toss in 4 quarts (16 cups) popped corn until coated. Press into a buttered sheet pan, let cool until firm, cut into squares and wrap in waxed paper.
note: Read in the Internet Archive OCR text. Elkhart and the 1900 date are from the library catalog record (place and date bracketed/unstated in the booklet; its text mentions 'more than thirty years' of the company's preparations, so it may be later, but well before 1929). It is a patent-medicine company's advertising booklet, not a community cookbook, and its sample letters come from other states.

title: Apple Butter With Cider
text: It usually takes about equal quantities of sweet cider and peeled and sliced apples to make butter the right consistency. In other words, two gallons of sweet cider should be boiled down to one gallon, and two gallons of peeled and sliced apples should be added to it either uncooked or as apple sauce. Two of the essentials of making good apple butter are long, slow cooking (four to six hours) and constant stirring. If sugar is used, it should be added after the cooking of cider and apples is about two-thirds done. ... Apple butter is spiced according to taste, about a half teaspoonful each of ground cinnamon, cloves and allspice being used for each gallon.
modern: Boil 2 quarts fresh sweet cider down to 1 quart, add 2 quarts peeled, sliced apples, and cook low and slow, stirring often, for several hours (a slow cooker or a 300°F oven with the lid ajar works well) until thick enough that it doesn't separate. Add about 1/2 to 1 cup sugar two-thirds of the way through if you like, and a pinch each of cinnamon, cloves and allspice at the end. Refrigerate, or can following current USDA guidance.
note: South Bend News-Times, 1 October 1917, page 7, via Hoosier State Chronicles (Indiana State Library). Read in the newspaper's OCR text; obvious OCR slips corrected ('swet', 'appla', 'beinp'). Faithful excerpt. The piece is a wartime bulletin from the National Emergency Food Garden Commission printed in the South Bend paper, not a local family recipe.

title: Doughnuts and silver: two kitchen hints
source_title: New Crumbs of Comfort: A Cook Book, compiled by the Ladies of St. Luke's Church ("Household Hints")
text: A spoonful of vinegar in a kettle of hot lard will prevent doughnuts from absorbing fat. ... A little dry salt will remove egg stains from silver.
modern: The vinegar trick is still passed around by doughnut makers. Keep the frying fat at 350–375°F; that matters most for doughnuts that aren't greasy. For silver, rub egg-tarnish spots with a pinch of salt on a damp cloth, then wash and dry.
note: Read in the Internet Archive OCR text (p. 177). The same page also lists hints using muriatic and oxalic acid; those were left out deliberately because they are poisons.

title: To take rust out of linen
source_title: New Crumbs of Comfort: A Cook Book, compiled by the Ladies of St. Luke's Church ("Household Hints")
text: Rust may be removed from linen by being covered with salt, wet thoroughly with lemon juice, and laid in the hot sun for several hours.
modern: This still works on white cotton and linen: sprinkle the spot with salt, soak it with fresh lemon juice, and leave it in strong sunlight for a few hours, then launder. Test colored fabric first, because lemon and sun can bleach it.
note: Read in the Internet Archive OCR text (p. 177); OCR 'Kust' corrected to 'Rust'.

title: Taking care of the ice chest
text: Keep the ice chest clean; wipe up anything spilled in it and, when necessary, wash it out with hot water, using two tablespoonfuls of washing soda to each gallon of water; rinse and dry thoroughly. ... Keep the ice compartment well filled. This is economy in the long run. Do not cover the ice with ice blankets, newspapers, or cloth. These prevent the ice melting, but make the ice chest less cool.
modern: The same idea works for a modern refrigerator or a camp cooler: keep it clean and full, and open the door as little as you can. A few tablespoons of baking soda in warm water is a gentler way to wash it out than washing soda.
note: Nappanee Advance-News, 11 August 1921, page 3, via Hoosier State Chronicles. Read in the newspaper's OCR text; obvious OCR slips corrected. Faithful excerpt. The item is credited in print to specialists of the United States Department of Agriculture (a syndicated household item printed in the Nappanee paper). The same page prints grape-juice desserts (Grape Sherbet, Grape Ice Cream) from the USDA.
